claim: Stringent response is a conserved bacterial stress response underlying virulence and antibiotic resistance.
source: Stringent response is a conserved bacterial stress response underlying virulence and antibiotic resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about bacterial stringent response and its role in pathogenesis.

claim: RelA/SpoT-homolog proteins synthesize transcriptional modulators (p)ppGpp, allowing bacteria to adapt to stress.
source: RelA/SpoT-homolog proteins synthesize transcriptional modulators (p)ppGpp, allowing bacteria to adapt to stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RSH protein function in bacterial stress response.

claim: RelA is activated during amino-acid starvation, when cognate deacyl-tRNA binds to the ribosomal A (aminoacyl-tRNA) site.
source: RelA is activated during amino-acid starvation, when cognate deacyl-tRNA binds to the ribosomal A (aminoacyl-tRNA) site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RelA activation mechanism.

claim: Four cryo-EM structures of E. coli RelA bound to the 70S ribosome were obtained at 3.9-Å to 4.1-Å resolution.
source: We report four cryo-EM structures of E. coli RelA bound to the 70S ribosome, in the absence and presence of deacyl-tRNA accommodating in the 30S A site.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The boomerang-shaped RelA has a wingspan of more than 100 Å.
source: The boomerang-shaped RelA with a wingspan of more than 100 Å wraps around the A/R (30S A-site/RelA-bound) tRNA.
evidence: This is a measurement derived from the structural data obtained in this study.

claim: The CCA end of the A/R tRNA pins the central TGS domain against the 30S subunit.
source: The CCA end of the A/R tRNA pins the central TGS domain against the 30S subunit, presenting the (p)ppGpp-synthetase domain near the 30S spur.
evidence: This structural observation is derived from the cryo-EM structures reported in the manuscript.

claim: The (p)ppGpp-synthetase domain is presented near the 30S spur.
source: The CCA end of the A/R tRNA pins the central TGS domain against the 30S subunit, presenting the (p)ppGpp-synthetase domain near the 30S spur.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The ribosome and A/R tRNA are captured in three conformations.
source: The ribosome and A/R tRNA are captured in three conformations, revealing hitherto elusive states of tRNA engagement with the ribosomal decoding center.
evidence: This is based on the structural data showing multiple conformational states.

claim: Decoding-center rearrangements are coupled with the step-wise 30S-subunit 'closure'.
source: Decoding-center rearrangements are coupled with the step-wise 30S-subunit 'closure', providing insights into the dynamics of high-fidelity tRNA decoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data showing coordinated conformational changes.

claim: RSH proteins play a central role in bacterial stringent response—a major stress-response pathway and key driver of bacterial virulence and antibiotic resistance.
source: RelA/SpoT homolog (RSH) proteins play a central role in bacterial stringent response—a major stress-response pathway and key driver of bacterial virulence and antibiotic resistance (Neidhardt, 1987; Gentry et al., 2000; Pizarro-Cerda and Tedin, 2004; Dalebroux et al., 2010a; Gao et al., 2010; Nguyen et al., 2011; Dordel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: RSH proteins synthesize small-molecule 'alarmones' collectively referred to as (p)ppGpp in response to environmental stress.
source: In response to environmental stress, such as nutrient deprivation, RSH proteins synthesize small-molecule 'alarmones' collectively referred to as (p)ppGpp (i.e., guanosine pentaphosphate and guanosine tetraphosphate; [Cashel and Gallant, 1969] and reviewed in [Potrykus and Cashel, 2008a; Atkinson et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Accumulation of (p)ppGpp activates transcription of genes required for stress response.
source: Accumulation of (p)ppGpp activates transcription of genes required for stress response, inhibits transcription of genes required for replication and growth, and reformats the transcription of metabolic genes according to the stress condition (Polakis et al., 1973; Mittenhuber, 2001; Magnusson et al., 2005; Jain et al., 2006a; Kuroda, 2006; Wang et al., 2007; Ferullo and Lovett, 2008; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008a; Traxler et al., 2008; Dalebroux et al., 2010a; Dalebroux et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Accumulation of (p)ppGpp inhibits transcription of genes required for replication and growth.
source: Accumulation of (p)ppGpp activates transcription of genes required for stress response, inhibits transcription of genes required for replication and growth, and reformats the transcription of metabolic genes according to the stress condition (Polakis et al., 1973; Mittenhuber, 2001; Magnusson et al., 2005; Jain et al., 2006a; Kuroda, 2006; Wang et al., 2007; Ferullo and Lovett, 2008; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008a; Traxler et al., 2008; Dalebroux et al., 2010a; Dalebroux et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Inactivation of RSH proteins in pathogenic bacteria dramatically reduces pathogenicity and bacterial load in the host, up to ~10,000-fold for Salmonella Typhimurium.
source: Inactivation of RSH proteins in pathogenic bacteria dramatically reduces pathogenicity and bacterial load in the host, up to ~10,000-fold for Salmonella Typhimurium (Na et al., 2006; Sun et al., 2009; Dalebroux et al., 2010a; Vogt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In E. coli, RelA synthesizes alarmones in response to amino acid deprivation.
source: In E. coli, RelA synthesizes alarmones in response to amino acid deprivation (Cashel and Gallant, 1969; Haseltine et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Binding of cognate but uncharged (deacylated) transfer RNA (tRNA) to the A (aminoacyl-tRNA) site of the 70S ribosome activates RelA.
source: When the supply of amino acids becomes limiting, binding of cognate but uncharged (deacylated) transfer RNA (tRNA) to the A (aminoacyl-tRNA) site of the 70S ribosome activates RelA (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Richter, 1976; Wendrich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complex triggers RelA to transfer a pyrophosphoryl group from ATP to GTP or to GDP to form pppGpp or ppGpp, respectively.
source: The 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complex triggers RelA to transfer a pyrophosphoryl group from ATP to GTP or to GDP to form pppGpp or ppGpp, respectively (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Sy and Lipmann, 1973; Wendrich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RelA binds to the ribosome in the absence of deacyl-tRNA, but this binding does not stimulate (p)ppGpp synthesis.
source: RelA also binds to the ribosome in the absence of deacyl-tRNA, but this binding does not stimulate (p)ppGpp synthesis (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Ramagopal and Davis, 1974; Wagner and Kurland, 1980; Wendrich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RelA is a 744 amino-acid protein (~84 kDa).
source: RelA, a 744 amino-acid protein (~84 kDa), consists of functionally distinct halves.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the protein's size.

claim: The N-terminal half of RelA includes a pseudo-hydrolase (inactive-hydrolase) domain (aa 1–200) and the (p)ppGpp synthetase domain (aa ~201–380).
source: The N-terminal half (amino acids 1–380) includes a pseudo-hydrolase (inactive-hydrolase) domain (aa 1–200) and the (p)ppGpp synthetase domain (aa ~201–380).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RelA domain organization.

claim: The synthetase domain belongs to the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily.
source: A crystal structure of the N-terminal half of the Streptococcus equisimilii RelA homolog RelSeq (aa 1–385) showed that the synthetase domain belongs to the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily and identified the catalytic residues (Hogg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The C-terminal half of RelA (aa ~400–744) is thought to control the synthetase activity of the N-terminal region.
source: The C-terminal half of RelA (aa ~400–744) and other RSH proteins is thought to control the synthetase activity of the N-terminal region (Schreiber et al., 1991; Gropp et al., 2001; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a; Mechold et al., 2002; Avarbock et al., 2005; Jain et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dimerization or oligomerization of free (ribosome-unbound) RelA and RSH proteins are thought to contribute to negative regulation of the synthetase activity.
source: Dimerization (Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a) or oligomerization (Gropp et al., 2001; Avarbock et al., 2005; Jain et al., 2006b) of free (ribosome-unbound) RelA and RSH proteins are thought to contribute to negative regulation of the synthetase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A 10.8-Å cryo-EM reconstruction of a 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complex revealed a bi-lobed density overlapping with the elongation-factor-binding site near the A site.
source: A 10.8-Å cryo-EM reconstruction of a 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complex revealed a bi-lobed density overlapping with the elongation-factor-binding site near the A site (Agirrezabala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The position of RelA and conformation of deacyl-tRNA in the 10.8-Å structure resembled those of elongation factor EF-Tu and aminoacyl tRNA in the 70S•EF-Tu•aa-tRNA pre-accommodation-like complexes.
source: The position of RelA and conformation of deacyl-tRNA resembled those of elongation factor EF-Tu and aminoacyl tRNA in the 70S•EF-Tu•aa-tRNA pre-accommodation-like complexes (Stark et al., 2002; Valle, 2002; Schmeing et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural work.

claim: The resolution of the 10.8-Å map did not allow model building.
source: However, the resolution of the map did not allow model building, leaving the molecular details of RelA activation unclear (Agirrezabala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Single-particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) and maximum-likelihood classification of a single dataset yielded four different cryo-EM structures of E. coli RelA bound to the E. coli ribosome at 3.9-Å to 4.1-Å resolution.
source: Single-particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) and maximum-likelihood classification of a single dataset yielded four different cryo-EM structures of E. coli RelA bound to the E. coli ribosome at 3.9-Å to 4.1-Å resolution.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and results obtained in this study.

claim: The local resolution of the maps in the ribosome core is higher than the average resolution of the maps.
source: As in cryo-EM structures of other ribosome complexes (e.g. [Greber et al., 2014; Fischer et al., 2015]), the local resolution of our maps in the ribosome core is higher than the average resolution of the maps, allowing for structural interpretation in central regions at near-atomic resolution.
evidence: This is based on data analysis and comparison with prior work.

claim: In all RelA-bound structures, the ribosome contains P-site and E-site tRNAs and adopts the classical, non-rotated conformation.
source: In all RelA-bound structures, the ribosome contains P-site and E-site tRNAs and adopts the classical, non-rotated conformation (Cate et al., 1999; Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Yusupov et al., 2001), similar to that of the post-translocation-ribosome with peptidyl-tRNA in the P site (Voorhees et al., 2009; Jenner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior work.

claim: In Structure I, the ribosome A site is vacant, and RelA is bound via its C-terminal portion while its N-terminal domains are disordered.
source: In Structure I, the ribosome A site is vacant, and RelA is bound via its C-terminal portion while its N-terminal domains are disordered (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In Structures II, III, and IV, the central and C-terminal parts of RelA are well resolved and the anticodon-stem loop (ASL) of a cognate deacyl-tRNAPhe is bound to the A site of the 30S subunit.
source: In Structures II, III, and IV, the central and C-terminal parts of RelA are well resolved and the anticodon-stem loop (ASL) of a cognate deacyl-tRNAPhe is bound to the A site of the 30S subunit (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: Structures II, III, and IV differ from each other in the conformations of RelA, A/R tRNA, the 30S subunit, and the L11 stalk of the 50S subunit.
source: Structures II, III, and IV differ from each other in the conformations of RelA, A/R tRNA, the 30S subunit, and the L11 stalk of the 50S subunit.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structural data.

claim: The N-terminus of ribosomal protein L11 is required for RelA activation in 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complexes.
source: The N-terminus of ribosomal protein L11 is required for RelA activation in 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complexes (Friesen et al., 1974; Parker et al., 1976; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001b; Wendrich et al., 2002; Jenvert and Holmberg Schiavone, 2007; Shyp et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The L11 N-terminus interacts with A/R tRNA but not with RelA in Structures II, III, and IV.
source: The L11 N-terminus interacts with A/R tRNA but not with RelA in Structures II, III, and IV (Figure 1F–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in the figures.

claim: The lack of (p)ppGpp synthetase activity of RelA on mutant ribosomes missing L11 or the L11 N-terminus is likely due to the inability of these ribosomes to coordinate deacyl-tRNA for activation of RelA.
source: Thus, the lack of (p)ppGpp synthetase activity of RelA on mutant ribosomes missing L11 or the L11 N-terminus (Friesen et al., 1974; Wendrich et al., 2002; Jenvert and Holmberg Schiavone, 2007) is likely due to the inability of these ribosomes to coordinate deacyl-tRNA for activation of RelA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and prior biochemical studies.

claim: The C-terminal region of RelA binds the intersubunit bridge B1a.
source: Specifically, the C-terminal region binds the intersubunit bridge B1a (Yusupov et al., 2001), which connects the A-site finger (helix 38) of the large subunit to the head of the small subunit (Figures 1E–G and 2A).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in the figures.

claim: The lack of density for the central and N-terminal domains of RelA in Structure I suggests that these regions are not ordered in the absence of deacylated A-site tRNA.
source: The lack of density for the central and N-terminal domains of RelA suggests that these regions are not ordered in the absence of deacylated A-site tRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The ACT domain is composed of four β-strands covered by two α-helices.
source: The ACT domain (aspartate kinase-chorismate mutase-tyrA; residues 665–744; [Atkinson et al., 2011]) is composed of four β-strands covered by two α-helices (Grant, 2006)
evidence: This is based on structural data and citation to prior work.

claim: The tips of two β-hairpins of the ACT domain, including Q705-Q706 and highly conserved D675, interact with R50 and R51 of L16.
source: The tips of two β-hairpins, including Q705-Q706 and highly conserved D675, interact with R50 and R51 of L16 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: The β-strands of ACT form a platform that packs against the 3´-strand of the A-site finger.
source: The β-strands of ACT form a platform that packs against the 3´-strand of the A-site finger.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The N-terminal and the C-terminal β-strands of ACT, including R670 and R739, interact with the bulged A896 of the A-site finger helix.
source: Here, the N-terminal and the C-terminal β-strands of ACT, including R670 and R739, interact with the bulged A896 of the A-site finger helix (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: The fold of the ACT domain resembles the RNP motif that binds single-stranded RNA.
source: The fold of the ACT domain was previously noted to resemble the RNP motif that binds single-stranded RNA, but no RNA-binding ACT domains had been identified (Burd and Dreyfuss, 1994; Grant, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The RelA ACT domain interacts with double-stranded RNA via the same face that RNP domains use to bind single-stranded RNA.
source: Our findings reveal that while the RelA ACT domain is not sequence-homologous to RNP motifs, it interacts with double-stranded RNA via the same face that RNP domains use to bind single-stranded RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: The RIS domain bridges the large and the small ribosomal subunits.
source: The domain bridges the large and the small ribosomal subunits (Figures 1E–F, 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The RIS domain core contains a four-stranded β-sheet and a short α-helix and is structurally similar to a zinc-finger domain.
source: The domain core contains a four-stranded β-sheet and a short α-helix and is structurally similar to a zinc-finger domain (Lee et al., 1989).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with known structures.

claim: On the 50S subunit, the α-helix of the RIS domain (residues 638–647) docks into the minor groove of the A-site finger and interacts with 23S rRNA residues 883–885 and 892–894.
source: On the 50S subunit, the α-helix (residues 638–647) docks into the minor groove of the A-site finger and interacts with 23S rRNA residues 883–885 and 892–894 (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: On the 30S subunit, the β-sheet of RIS packs at the hydrophobic patch of the β-sheet of S19, comprising V57, P58 and F60.
source: On the 30S subunit, the β-sheet of RIS packs at the hydrophobic patch of the β-sheet of S19, comprising V57, P58 and F60.
evidence: This is based on structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: Structure I reveals that the ACT and RIS domains of RelA form a C-terminal superdomain that anchors RelA to the 70S ribosome.
source: In summary, Structure I reveals that the ACT and RIS domains of RelA form a C-terminal superdomain that anchors RelA to the 70S ribosome, consistent with reduced binding of RelA to ribosomes upon mutation or deletion of the C-terminal domain (Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior biochemical studies.

claim: The density for the RIS domain core is well resolved in Structure I.
source: The density for the RIS domain core is well resolved in Structure I (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), supporting the model that amino acids encompassing the RIS domain form the major ribosomal-binding domain of RelA (Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior work.

claim: The positions of A/R tRNA in the RelA-bound structures globally resemble that of the A/T pre-accommodated aminoacyl-tRNA captured in the ribosome in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: As described in the earlier cryo-EM study of RelA ribosome complexes (Agirrezabala et al., 2013), the positions of A/R tRNA in the RelA-bound structures globally resemble that of the A/T pre-accommodated aminoacyl-tRNA captured in the ribosome in the presence of EF-Tu (Stark et al., 2002; Valle, 2002; Schmeing et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: RelA wraps around the tRNA and adopts a boomerang-like conformation in Structures II, III, and IV.
source: In these structures, RelA wraps around the tRNA and adopts a boomerang-like conformation (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The extended RelA conformation contrasts with the compact RelA conformation occupying the elongation-factor binding site that was proposed based on the 10.8-Å map.
source: This RelA conformation contrasts with the compact RelA conformation occupying the elongation-factor binding site that was proposed based on the 10.8-Å map of a 70S•RelA•deacyl-tRNA complex (Agirrezabala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work.

claim: Re-evaluation of the lower-resolution map revealed previously unassigned density near the intersubunit bridge B1a, which makes that map consistent with the extended RelA conformation.
source: However, our re-evaluation of the lower-resolution map revealed previously unassigned density near the intersubunit bridge B1a, which makes that map consistent with the extended RelA conformation shown here (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of prior data.

claim: In Structures II, III and IV, the C-terminal RIS and ACT domains form one wing of the boomerang-like structure at bridge B1a and are positioned similarly to those in Structure I.
source: In Structures II, III and IV, the C-terminal RIS and ACT domains form one wing of the boomerang-like structure at bridge B1a and are positioned similarly to those in Structure I (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The C-terminal domains are connected with the central α-helical domain (AH; aa 485–580).
source: The C-terminal domains are connected with the central α-helical domain (AH; aa 485–580; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The core of the AH domain (aa ~520–560) is formed by short helices, which pack near the D stem of the A/R tRNA.
source: The core of the AH domain (aa ~520–560) is formed by short helices, which pack near the D stem of the A/R tRNA.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The ~15-amino-acid C-terminal helix of the AH domain connects the AH core with the RIS domain (Linker helix 2).
source: The ~15-amino-acid C-terminal helix of the AH domain connects the AH core with the RIS domain (Linker helix 2; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: Linker helix 2 packs against the ACT domain similarly to an α-helix of the dimerization partner of the isolated ACT domain of Chlorobium tepidum RSH.
source: Linker helix 2 packs against the ACT domain similarly to an α-helix of the dimerization partner of the isolated ACT domain of Chlorobium tepidum RSH (PDB: 2KO1; [Eletsky et al., 2009]) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: If the ACT domains were dimerized in the full-length free RelA, the packing of Linker helix 2 next to the ACT domain would be possible on the ribosome only upon dimer disassembly.
source: This suggests that if the ACT domains were also dimerized in the full-length free RelA, the packing of this α-helical linker next to the ACT domain would be possible on the ribosome only upon dimer disassembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: The long N-terminal helix (Linker Helix 1) lies under the acceptor arm of the A/R tRNA and connects the AH core with the ubiquitin-like TGS domain (amino acids 405–470).
source: The long N-terminal helix (Linker Helix 1), which lies under the acceptor arm of the A/R tRNA, connects the AH core with the ubiquitin-like TGS domain (amino acids 405–470; ThrRS, GTPase, and SpoT/RelA (Sankaranarayanan et al., 1999) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The central AH and TGS domains form the elbow of the RelA boomerang.
source: Together the central AH and TGS domains form the elbow of the RelA boomerang.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The TGS domain is pinned against 16S rRNA by the acceptor end of A/R tRNA.
source: The TGS domain is pinned against 16S rRNA by the acceptor end of A/R tRNA (Figure 3A–B), as described below.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The overall conformations of the TGS domain are similar between Structures II, III, and IV.
source: The overall conformations of the TGS domain are similar between Structures II, III, and IV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The N-terminal pseudo-hydrolase domain (aa 1–200) and synthetase domain (aa 200–380) form the second wing of the boomerang and face the periphery of the ribosome in the vicinity of the 30S subunit spur (helix 6).
source: Finally, the N-terminal pseudo-hydrolase domain (aa 1–200) and synthetase domain (aa 200–380), forming the second wing of the boomerang, face the periphery of the ribosome in the vicinity of the 30S subunit spur (helix 6) (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The N-terminal domains adopt a range of conformations in Structures II, III and IV.
source: Finally, the N-terminal pseudo-hydrolase domain (aa 1–200) and synthetase domain (aa 200–380), forming the second wing of the boomerang, face the periphery of the ribosome in the vicinity of the 30S subunit spur (helix 6) (Figure 4A) and adopt a range of conformations in Structures II, III and IV, as discussed below.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The TGS domain interacts with the 3´ CCA end of deacylated A/R tRNA and with 16S rRNA helix 5.
source: The TGS domain interacts with the 3´ CCA end of deacylated A/R tRNA and with 16S rRNA helix 5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The 74CCA76 end adopts a conformation similar to that in the EF-Tu-bound A/T-tRNA, in which C75 is bulged out.
source: The 74CCA76 end adopts a conformation similar to that in the EF-Tu-bound A/T-tRNA, in which C75 is bulged out (Schmeing et al., 2009; Fischer et al., 2015), whereas C74 and A76 interact with several conserved residues of the protein.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: H432 stabilizes the CCA conformation by intercalating between C74 and C75.
source: H432 stabilizes the CCA conformation by intercalating between C74 and C75 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: P411 and K412 on a β-hairpin loop interact with the nucleobase of A76.
source: P411 and K412 on a β-hairpin loop interact with the nucleobase of A76 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The ribose of A76 faces a β-sheet at residues 461–465.
source: The ribose of A76 faces a β-sheet at residues 461–465 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA requires deacyl-tRNA binding to the ribosome.
source: (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA requires deacyl-tRNA binding to the ribosome (Haseltine and Block, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An amino acid bound at A76 would sterically clash with the β-sheet of TGS and prevent binding of A/R tRNA to the TGS domain.
source: An amino acid bound at A76 would sterically clash with the β-sheet of TGS and prevent binding of A/R tRNA to the TGS domain, in keeping with the inability of charged tRNA to activate RelA.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: The isolated TGS domain from C. leptum RSH forms a dimer.
source: To gain insights into the role of interaction between the CCA end and the TGS domain, we compared our structures with the X-ray structure of the isolated TGS domain from C. leptum RSH (PDB: 3HVZ) (Forouhar et al., 2009). The isolated TGS domain forms a dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The A/R tRNA disrupts the dimerization interface of the isolated TGS domain.
source: The comparison reveals that the A/R tRNA disrupts the dimerization interface (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Oligomerization of RSH proteins inhibits (p)ppGpp production.
source: Since oligomerization of RSH proteins inhibits (p)ppGpp production (Gropp et al., 2001; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a; Avarbock et al., 2005; Jain et al., 2006b), interaction with deacyl-tRNA may contribute to RelA activation via stabilization of the monomeric RelA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interaction with deacyl-tRNA may contribute to RelA activation via stabilization of the monomeric RelA.
source: Since oligomerization of RSH proteins inhibits (p)ppGpp production (Gropp et al., 2001; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a; Avarbock et al., 2005; Jain et al., 2006b), interaction with deacyl-tRNA may contribute to RelA activation via stabilization of the monomeric RelA.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural data and prior research.

claim: The N-terminal pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domains in the intersubunit space of the ribosome were poorly resolved in the maps for Structures II, III and IV, suggesting structural heterogeneity.
source: The N-terminal pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domains in the intersubunit space of the ribosome were poorly resolved in the maps for Structures II, III and IV, suggesting structural heterogeneity.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: Sub-classification revealed two predominant classes of N-terminal domain conformations that differ in position by at least 10 Å.
source: Sub-classification of each structure into three or more classes revealed two predominant classes that resolved the shapes of the N-terminal region, which differ in position by at least 10 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is based on data sub-classification analysis.

claim: Classification into seven classes reveals the appearance of less resolved density between the two extreme conformations, suggesting that the N-terminal domain samples a continuum of positions.
source: Classification into seven classes reveals the appearance of less resolved density between these two extreme conformations, suggesting that the N-terminal domain samples a continuum of positions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on data sub-classification analysis and interpretation.

claim: In the first conformation, the synthetase domain is positioned near the spur.
source: In the first conformation, the synthetase domain is positioned near the spur.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The synthetase domain contains a long helix (the spine helix, at aa 208–243), which buttresses the catalytic region at the β-platform (aa 248–340).
source: The synthetase domain contains a long helix (the spine helix, at aa 208–243), which buttresses the catalytic region at the β-platform (aa 248–340; Figure 4A and C) (Hogg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on structural data and citation to prior work.

claim: The loop connecting the spine helix with the β-platform (at residues 244–246) approaches the tip of the 16S spur within ~5 Å.
source: The loop, which connects the spine helix with the β-platform (at residues 244–246) approaches the tip of the 16S spur within ~5 Å, suggesting that the protein interacts with rRNA, but the details of the possible interaction cannot be visualized in the low-resolution maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: In the second conformation, the synthetase domain is separated from the spur by shifting away from its first predominant conformation by ~10 Å.
source: In the second conformation, the synthetase domain is separated from the spur by shifting away from its first predominant conformation by ~10 Å (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The pseudo-hydrolase domain is bound near the sarcin-ricin loop of the large subunit (nt 2653–2667 of 23S rRNA).
source: The pseudo-hydrolase domain is bound near the sarcin-ricin loop of the large subunit (nt 2653–2667 of 23S rRNA).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The homologous RelSeq contains a functional hydrolase domain, and allosteric regulation was proposed to govern the switch between (p)ppGpp hydrolase and synthetase activities.
source: The homologous RelSeq contains a functional hydrolase domain, and allosteric regulation was proposed to govern the switch between (p)ppGpp hydrolase and synthetase activities (Hogg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of the synthetase domain of RelA may involve conformational rearrangements between the pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domains, triggered by movement relative to the TGS domain and/or interactions with ribosomal RNA.
source: It is possible that activation of the synthetase domain of RelA involves conformational rearrangements between the pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domains, triggered by movement relative to the TGS domain and/or interactions with ribosomal RNA.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Specific interactions of the synthetase domain with the spur may trigger the catalytic activity.
source: Alternatively, specific interactions of the synthetase domain with the spur may trigger the catalytic activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural observations.

claim: The RelA synthetase domain structure resembles that of other second-messenger synthetases, including metazoan innate immune sensor OAS1, metazoan cGAS, and Vibrio cholerae pathogenicity factor DncV.
source: The RelA synthetase domain structure resembles that of other second-messenger synthetases (Figures 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), including: metazoan innate immune sensor OAS1, a 2′–5′–oligoadenylate synthase triggered by double-stranded RNA (Donovan et al., 2013; Lohöfener et al., 2015); metazoan cGAS, a cyclic-GMP–2′–5′–AMP synthase triggered by double-stranded DNA (Civril et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2013; Kranzusch et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013); and Vibrio cholerae pathogenicity factor DncV, a cyclic-GMP–3′–5′–AMP synthase (Kranzusch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: Innate immune sensors OAS1 and cGAS are activated by binding of an RNA or DNA duplex, respectively, at the spine helix.
source: Innate immune sensors OAS1 and cGAS are activated by binding of an RNA or DNA duplex, respectively, at the spine helix (Civril et al., 2013; Donovan et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2013; Lohöfener et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The proximity of the spine helix of RelA to the spur highlights the possibility of activation of RelA via a mechanism reminiscent of those for OAS1 and cGAS innate immune sensors.
source: The proximity of the spine helix of RelA to the spur highlights the possibility of activation of RelA via a mechanism reminiscent of those for OAS1 and cGAS innate immune sensors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural comparison.

claim: The structures reveal three conformations of the deacyl-tRNA and the 30S decoding center.
source: Our structures reveal three conformations of the deacyl-tRNA and the 30S decoding center, providing insights into the mechanism of specific RelA activation by cognate tRNA (shown as an animation in Video 1 and http://labs.umassmed.edu/korostelevlab/msc/relamovie.gif).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: Activation of (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA on the ribosome depends on the selection of tRNA cognate to the mRNA codon in the A site.
source: Activation of (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA on the ribosome depends on the selection of tRNA cognate to the mRNA codon in the A site (Haseltine and Block, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Substitution of cognate tRNAAla with near-cognate tRNAVal or tRNAGlu results in a more than 32-fold decrease in (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA on ribosomes programmed with an Ala codon in the A site.
source: In their in vitro experiments, Haseltine and Block demonstrated that the substitution of cognate tRNAAla, which reads the GCA, GCC, GCG or GCU codons, with near-cognate tRNAVal (GUA, GUC, GUG, or GUU) or tRNAGlu (GAA or GAG) results in a more than 32-fold decrease in (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA on ribosomes programmed with an Ala codon in the A site (Haseltine and Block, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The structures suggest stepwise accommodation of the codon-anticodon helix in the decoding center.
source: Our structures suggest stepwise accommodation of the codon-anticodon helix in the decoding center, which helps explain this exquisite sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: Classification of the cryo-EM data revealed three unique classes (Structures II, III, and IV) that differ in the conformation of A/R tRNA.
source: Classification of our cryo-EM data revealed three unique classes (Structures II, III, and IV) that differ in the conformation of A/R tRNA (Figures 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on data classification analysis.

claim: In all three structures, the A/R tRNA anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon in the 30S A site, the elbow contacts the L11 stalk, whereas the acceptor arm is located in the vicinity of the sarcin-ricin loop of 23S rRNA.
source: In all three structures, the A/R tRNA anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon in the 30S A site, the elbow contacts the L11 stalk, whereas the acceptor arm is located in the vicinity of the sarcin-ricin loop of 23S rRNA (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The A/R tRNAs are highly distorted relative to accommodated A-site tRNA, such that the anticodon-stem loop is kinked toward the CCA end of the tRNA.
source: The A/R tRNAs are highly distorted relative to accommodated A-site tRNA, such that the anticodon-stem loop is kinked toward the CCA end of the tRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), somewhat similar to the A/T aminoacyl-tRNA in EF-Tu-bound pre-accommodation-like ribosome structures (Stark et al., 2002; Valle, 2002; Schmeing et al., 2009; Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The A/R tRNAs differ from the A/T tRNA in the degrees of twisting around residues 26 and 44.
source: The A/R tRNAs, however, differ from the A/T tRNA in the degrees of twisting around residues 26 and 44, which link the anticodon-stem loop with the rest of tRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The CCA end of A/R tRNA (Structure II) is positioned ~10 Å away from that in the A/T tRNA.
source: The CCA end of A/R tRNA (Structure II) is positioned ~10 Å away from that in the A/T tRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Relative to the P-site tRNA, the A/R elbows of all three RelA-bound structures are tilted by up to 10 Å farther than the A/T tRNA.
source: Relative to the P-site tRNA, the A/R elbows of all three RelA-bound structures are tilted by up to 10 Å farther than the A/T tRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Comparison of Structures II, III, and IV reveals a concerted movement of A/R tRNA and the RelA central domains toward the head of the 30S subunit.
source: Comparison of Structures II, III, and IV reveals a concerted movement of A/R tRNA and the RelA central domains toward the head of the 30S subunit, as if the tRNA gradually 'settles' into the A site of the 30S subunit from Structure II through III to IV (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The tRNA accommodation coincides with a conformational change in the 30S subunit termed 'domain closure'.
source: The tRNA accommodation coincides with a conformational change in the 30S subunit termed 'domain closure' (Ogle et al., 2001; Ogle et al., 2002; Jenner et al., 2010; Demeshkina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior work.

claim: The acceptor arm of A/R tRNA and the TGS domain of RelA shift toward the head of the 30S subunit by ~2 Å between Structures II and III, and by ~2 Å between Structures III and IV.
source: The acceptor arm of A/R tRNA and the TGS domain of RelA shift toward the head of the 30S subunit by ~2 Å between Structures II and III, and by ~2 Å between Structures III and IV (Figure 5C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The shoulder of the 30S subunit moves by nearly 5 Å toward the head and body from Structure II to IV.
source: The shoulder of the 30S subunit also moves by nearly 5 Å toward the head and body from Structure II to IV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: In Structure II, the 30S subunit is in the open conformation observed previously in the absence of A-site tRNA.
source: In Structure II, the 30S subunit is in the open conformation observed previously in the absence of A-site tRNA (Ogle et al., 2001; Jenner et al., 2010), whereas in Structure IV, the 30S subunit is in the fully closed conformation (Figure 6A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Selmer et al., 2006; Jenner et al., 2010; Demeshkina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: In Structure IV, the 30S subunit is in the fully closed conformation.
source: In Structure II, the 30S subunit is in the open conformation observed previously in the absence of A-site tRNA (Ogle et al., 2001; Jenner et al., 2010), whereas in Structure IV, the 30S subunit is in the fully closed conformation (Figure 6A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Selmer et al., 2006; Jenner et al., 2010; Demeshkina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: The 30S subunit in Structure III adopts an intermediate state between the open and closed states.
source: The 30S subunit in Structure III adopts an intermediate state between the open and closed states (Figures 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Structure II represents a previously unseen open 30S subunit in the presence of the codon-anticodon interaction.
source: Thus, Structure II represents a previously unseen open 30S subunit in the presence of the codon-anticodon interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: Structure III represents an intermediate in the 30S 'domain-closure' pathway.
source: Structure III, in turn, represents an intermediate in the 30S 'domain-closure' pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: The local resolution of the maps in the decoding center is sufficient to determine nucleotide conformations.
source: The local resolution of our maps in the decoding center is sufficient to determine nucleotide conformations (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: Universally conserved nucleotides of the decoding center A1492, A1493, G530 of 16S rRNA and A1913 of 23S rRNA interact with the minor groove of the codon-anticodon interaction.
source: Studies of ribosome-tRNA complexes demonstrated that the decoding center plays a central role in cognate tRNA stabilization. Specifically, universally conserved nucleotides of the decoding center A1492, A1493, G530 of 16S rRNA and A1913 of 23S rRNA interact with the minor groove of the codon-anticodon interaction (Ogle et al., 2001; Selmer et al., 2006; Jenner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A1492 and A1493 are important in stabilizing Watson-Crick geometry of the first two base pairs.
source: A1492 and A1493 are important in stabilizing Watson-Crick geometry of the first two base pairs (Ogle et al., 2001; Demeshkina et al., 2012), and are thus thought to contribute to tRNA recognition, providing high fidelity of protein synthesis (Ogle et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In Structure II, the conformation of the decoding center resembles that found in the absence of an A-site tRNA with the 30S in an open conformation.
source: Despite the presence of an A-site tRNA in Structure II, the conformation of the decoding center resembles that found in the absence of an A-site tRNA with the 30S in an open conformation (compare Figure 6E–D) (Ogle et al., 2001; Jenner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: In Structure II, A1492 resides inside helix 44 (A1492 OFF).
source: Strong density shows that A1492 resides inside helix 44, as observed in the absence of an A-site tRNA (A1492 OFF) (Ogle et al., 2001; Jenner et al., 2010) (Figures 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,F and I).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior work.

claim: In Structure II, G530 is separated from A1492 by more than 10 Å (G530 in the OFF position).
source: G530 is separated from A1492 by more than 10 Å (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B), similar to that in the absence of an A-site tRNA (G530 in the OFF position).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: In Structure II, A1493 bulges out from helix 44 of 16S rRNA and is oriented toward the codon-anticodon helix (A1493 in the ON position).
source: A1493 bulges out from helix 44 of 16S rRNA, so that the nucleotide is oriented toward the codon-anticodon helix. Weak density suggests that the base does not form a stable interaction with the codon-anticodon helix (Figure 6—figure supplement 3I), although A1493 appears pre-arranged for such an interaction by being bulged out (A1493 in the ON position).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: In Structure III, A1493 and A1492 contact the codon-anticodon helix, forming A-minor interactions with the first and second codon-anticodon base pairs (A1493 ON and A1492 ON).
source: In the decoding center of Structure III — corresponding to the intermediate state of domain closure — A1493 and A1492 contact the codon-anticodon helix, forming A-minor interactions with the first and second codon-anticodon base pairs (i.e., A1493 ON and A1492 ON; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: In Structure III, G530 is in the anti conformation and shifted toward A1492 (G530 SEMI-ON).
source: G530 is in the anti conformation and shifted, along with the shoulder of the 30S subunit, toward A1492 (Figures 6C,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3C,G,J). Here, G530 adopts a position between that in ribosomes with 'vacant' and 'filled' A sites (G530 SEMI-ON).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: In Structure IV, the decoding-center nucleotides adopt conformations nearly identical to those in the A-tRNA-bound ribosome (A1493/A1492/G530 ON).
source: Finally, the decoding-center nucleotides in Structure IV adopt conformations nearly identical (Figures 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3D, H, K) to those in the A-tRNA-bound ribosome (A1493/A1492/G530 ON) (Selmer et al., 2006; Jenner et al., 2010; Demeshkina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: In Structure IV, the 530 loop is shifted closer to A1493 and A1492, so that G530 interacts with A1492.
source: The 530 loop is shifted closer to A1493 and A1492, so that G530 interacts with A1492.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The shift of the 530 loop is coupled with the 30S subunit closure.
source: This shift is coupled with the 30S subunit closure, also observed in 70S complexes with A-site tRNA (Selmer et al., 2006; Jenner et al., 2010; Demeshkina et al., 2012) and pre-accommodation-like 70S•EF-Tu•aa-tRNA complexes (Stark et al., 2002; Valle, 2002; Schmeing et al., 2009; Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior work.

claim: At early steps, interaction of the anticodon stem loop of a cognate or non-cognate tRNA occurs with the domain-open conformation of the 30S subunit, in which the decoding nucleotides are not positioned to stabilize the codon-anticodon helix.
source: We propose the following structural mechanism of deacyl-tRNA decoding (Video 1 and Figure 7). At early steps, interaction of the anticodon stem loop of a cognate or non-cognate tRNA occurs with the domain-open conformation of the 30S subunit, in which the decoding nucleotides are not positioned to stabilize the codon-anticodon helix.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: At the early stage, the non-cognate tRNA dissociates prior to the closure of the 30S subunit.
source: At this stage, the non-cognate tRNA dissociates prior to the closure of the 30S subunit, as the latter would require formation of the A-minor interactions by A1492 and A1493 with the Watson-Crick-paired codon-anticodon helix (Ogle et al., 2001; Jenner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data and prior work.

claim: In the case of cognate tRNA, acceptance of tRNA and 30S domain closure would be coupled with the formation of the A1492-G530 bridge (G530 ON) to stabilize the tRNA on the ribosome.
source: In the case of cognate tRNA, acceptance of tRNA and 30S domain closure would be coupled with the formation of the A1492-G530 bridge (i.e., G530 ON) to stabilize the tRNA on the ribosome.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: The A1493-ON and/or A1493/A1492-ON states in Structures II and III may serve as checkpoints on the path of acceptance of Watson-Crick base-paired tRNA and mRNA.
source: The A1493-ON and/or A1493/A1492-ON states in Structures II and III may therefore serve as checkpoints on the path of acceptance of Watson-Crick base-paired tRNA and mRNA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: The observation of previously elusive states of tRNA binding suggests insights into the accuracy of aminoacyl-tRNA selection during elongation.
source: Our observation of previously elusive states of tRNA binding also suggests insights into the accuracy of aminoacyl-tRNA selection during elongation, a universally conserved mechanism responsible for the accurate transfer of genetic information.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: Current structural understanding of tRNA selection is limited to observation of the open and the closed conformations of the 30S subunit in the absence and presence of A-site tRNA, respectively.
source: Current structural understanding is limited to observation of the open and the closed conformations of the 30S subunit in the absence and presence of A-site tRNA, respectively (Ogle et al., 2001; Jenner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Biochemical and biophysical studies demonstrated that tRNA accommodation includes an early short-lived intermediate – prior to forming the A/T state – during which non-cognate tRNAs can be rejected.
source: Biochemical (Rodnina et al., 1994; Rodnina et al., 1995; Rodnina et al., 1996; Pape et al., 1998) and biophysical (Blanchard et al., 2004; Gonzalez et al., 2007) studies demonstrated that tRNA accommodation includes an early short-lived intermediate – prior to forming the A/T state – during which non-cognate tRNAs can be rejected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Early or intermediate states prior to the formation of the A/T state have not been structurally visualized at high resolution before this work.
source: However, early or intermediate states prior to the formation of the A/T state have not been structurally visualized at high resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: The observation of incompletely engaged tRNA in the domain-open or intermediate state of the 30S subunit suggests that similar states exist for the aminoacyl-tRNA•EF-Tu•GTP ternary complex.
source: Our observation of incompletely engaged tRNA in the domain-open or intermediate state of the 30S subunit suggests that similar states exist for the aminoacyl-tRNA•EF-Tu•GTP ternary complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: The tRNA acceptor arm positions are separated by ~5 Å in the early pre-accommodation step (Structure II) and the domain-closed step tRNA (Structure IV).
source: The tRNA acceptor arm positions are separated by ~5 Å in the early pre-accommodation step (Structure II) and the domain-closed step tRNA (Structure IV).
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The separation of tRNA acceptor arm positions could be sufficient to keep EF-Tu farther from the GTPase-activating sarcin-ricin loop of 23S rRNA at an early step, allowing non-cognate ternary complex dissociation prior to GTP hydrolysis, EF-Tu release and tRNA acceptance via domain closure.
source: This could be sufficient to keep EF-Tu farther from the GTPase-activating sarcin-ricin loop of 23S rRNA (Voorhees et al., 2010) at an early step, allowing non-cognate ternary complex dissociation prior to GTP hydrolysis, EF-Tu release and tRNA acceptance via domain closure.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural data and prior work.

claim: The stringent response must be rapidly initiated upon cellular stress.
source: The stringent response must be rapidly initiated upon cellular stress (Cashel and Gallant, 1969), but under normal conditions the basal activity of RelA must remain low to avoid cell growth inhibition by (p)ppGpp (Schreiber et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Under normal conditions the basal activity of RelA must remain low to avoid cell growth inhibition by (p)ppGpp.
source: The stringent response must be rapidly initiated upon cellular stress (Cashel and Gallant, 1969), but under normal conditions the basal activity of RelA must remain low to avoid cell growth inhibition by (p)ppGpp (Schreiber et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The cellular concentration of RelA under normal conditions is several orders of magnitude lower than that of ribosomes.
source: The cellular concentration of RelA under normal conditions is several orders of magnitude lower than that of ribosomes (Pedersen and Kjeldgaard, 1977; Justesen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Biochemical studies show that ribosomes bound with EF-Tu•GDPCP•Phe-tRNAPhe ternary complex can also bind RelA but do not result in (p)ppGpp synthesis.
source: Biochemical studies show that ribosomes bound with EF-Tu•GDPCP•Phe-tRNAPhe ternary complex can also bind RelA but do not result in (p)ppGpp synthesis (Richter et al., 1975; Wendrich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Superimposing E. coli 70S EF-Tu•GDP•Phe-tRNAPhe•kirromycin complex onto Structure I reveals no clashes between EF-Tu ternary complex and the RelA RIS and ACT domains.
source: Superimposing E. coli 70S EF-Tu•GDP•Phe-tRNAPhe•kirromycin complex (Fischer et al., 2015) onto our 70S•RelA Structure I reveals no clashes between EF-Tu ternary complex and the RelA RIS and ACT domains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The early steps of elongation are compatible with a ribosome-bound but inactive RelA.
source: Thus, the early steps of elongation are compatible with a ribosome-bound but inactive RelA.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and prior biochemical studies.

claim: Full accommodation and translocation of tRNA would require displacement or relocation of RelA from bridge B1a.
source: Full accommodation and translocation of tRNA, however, would require displacement or relocation of RelA from bridge B1a, where the C-terminal superdomain is bound.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: When Structure I is superimposed with the structure of the 70S ribosome bound with three tRNAs, there is a prominent steric clash between the ACT domain and the fully accommodated A-site tRNA.
source: When we superimpose Structure I and the structure of the 70S ribosome bound with three tRNAs (Jenner et al., 2010) (PDB: 3I8H), we observe a prominent steric clash between the ACT domain and the fully accommodated A-site tRNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: RelA does not bind pre-translocation and post-translocation 70S•EF-G complexes.
source: Moreover, RelA does not bind pre-translocation and post-translocation 70S•EF-G complexes (Wagner and Kurland, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Binding of EF-G to the pre-translocation ribosome stabilizes a rotated intersubunit state.
source: Binding of EF-G to the pre-translocation ribosome stabilizes a rotated intersubunit state (Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Cornish et al., 2008; Brilot et al., 2013), in which bridge B1a is restructured and S19 is relocated by ~20 Å because of 30S subunit rotation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The rotated conformation would disrupt the contact between the RIS domain and S19 and prevent binding of RelA to the rotated EF-G-bound ribosomes.
source: This conformation would disrupt the contact between the RIS domain and S19 and prevent binding of RelA to the rotated EF-G-bound ribosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: In the non-rotated post-translocation ribosome, steric hindrance between EF-G domain IV and Linker Helix 2 may prevent RelA from binding.
source: In the non-rotated post-translocation ribosome, wherein EF-G occupies the A site of the 30S subunit (Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Gao et al., 2009), steric hindrance between EF-G domain IV and Linker Helix 2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) may prevent RelA from binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: In translating ribosomes, RelA cannot be activated and must be displaced from its binding site near bridge B1a.
source: Thus, in translating ribosomes, RelA cannot be activated and must be displaced from its binding site near bridge B1a.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and prior biochemical studies.

claim: The C-terminal domains of RelA associate with the ribosome near bridge B1a, as in Structure I.
source: Our structures suggest the following mechanism of RelA activation (Figure 7). The C-terminal domains of RelA associate with the ribosome near bridge B1a, as in Structure I.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: During amino-acid starvation, a cognate deacyl-tRNA binds the 30S A site as the codon-anticodon interaction is stabilized following step-wise rearrangements of the decoding center.
source: During amino-acid starvation, a cognate deacyl-tRNA binds the 30S A site as the codon-anticodon interaction is stabilized following step-wise rearrangements of the decoding center, as in Structures II, III and IV.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: The deacylated CCA end pins the TGS domain against the body of the 30S subunit, exposing the dynamic synthetase domain near the spur.
source: At the other end of the tRNA, the deacylated CCA end pins the TGS domain against the body of the 30S subunit, exposing the dynamic synthetase domain near the spur.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: Stabilization of RelA in the 70S•deacyl-tRNA complex alleviates the autoinhibition of the synthetase activity observed in ribosome-free RelA.
source: First, stabilization of RelA in the 70S•deacyl-tRNA complex alleviates the autoinhibition of the synthetase activity observed in ribosome-free RelA (Schreiber et al., 1991; Gropp et al., 2001; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data and prior research.

claim: If the autoinhibition is due to inter-molecular interactions in oligomeric RelA, the dimerization surfaces of the ACT and TGS domains become disrupted by the ordering of the AH domain and interaction with the CCA end of the A/R tRNA, respectively.
source: If the autoinhibition is due to inter-molecular interactions in oligomeric RelA (Gropp et al., 2001; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001a), as suggested by structures of free dimeric ACT (Eletsky et al., 2009) and TGS domains (Forouhar et al., 2009), the dimerization surfaces of the ACT and TGS domains become disrupted by the ordering of the AH domain (Figure 2D) and interaction with the CCA end of the A/R tRNA (Figure 3C), respectively.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data and prior research.

claim: Changes in the relative positions of the pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domain, and/or in the interaction of the synthetase domains with the spur may contribute to the catalytic activation of the (p)ppGpp synthetase.
source: Second, consistent with the observation of several conformations of the catalytic N-terminal domain, changes in the relative positions of the pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domain, and/or in the interaction of the synthetase domains with the spur may contribute to the catalytic activation of the (p)ppGpp synthetase.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: During translation under unstressed conditions, aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation in the A site and ribosome translocation displaces the C-terminus of RelA from the ribosome or at least from bridge B1a.
source: During translation under unstressed conditions, however, aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation in the A site and ribosome translocation displaces the C-terminus of RelA from the ribosome or at least from bridge B1a.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: Density for RelA is not observed when an A-site tRNA is fully accommodated.
source: We do not observe density for RelA when an A-site tRNA is fully accommodated, consistent with the model that RelA is displaced from the ribosome.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: The structure-based mechanism is consistent with models in which RelA produces (p)ppGpp when bound to ribosomes with cognate deacylated tRNA, but is actively displaced from ribosomes during translation to limit (p)ppGpp production.
source: Our structure-based mechanism is consistent with models in which RelA produces (p)ppGpp when bound to ribosomes with cognate deacylated tRNA, but is actively displaced from ribosomes during translation to limit (p)ppGpp production (Elf and Ehrenberg, 2005; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and comparison with prior models.

claim: Structure I suggests that the presence of tRNA is not necessary for RelA binding.
source: Although RelA binding to the 70S ribosome following deacyl-tRNA is possible, our Structure I suggests that the presence of tRNA is not necessary for RelA binding, in agreement with biochemical observations (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Ramagopal and Davis, 1974; Wagner and Kurland, 1980; Wendrich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with prior biochemical studies.

claim: The structures indicate that RelA can bind a stalled (non-translating) ribosome before deacyl-tRNA arrives and that deacyl-tRNA binding is required to stabilize the extended RelA conformation.
source: Our structures, by contrast, indicate that RelA can bind a stalled (non-translating) ribosome before deacyl-tRNA arrives and that deacyl-tRNA binding is required to stabilize the extended RelA conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: RelA might be prepared for catalysis in all three A/R-tRNA–bound states.
source: RelA might be prepared for catalysis in all three states.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Continuous transitions between Structures II, III, and IV could be required for synthesis of (p)ppGpp.
source: Alternatively, continuous transitions between Structures II, III, and IV could be required for synthesis of (p)ppGpp, for example, by distributing the alignment of catalytic residues, substrate binding and positioning, and product release between these distinct states.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: RelA is activated by only one state, likely Structure IV.
source: A third model is that RelA is activated by only one state. We favor mechanisms, in which Structure IV is required to activate RelA, either as part of an 'activating' ensemble or as a sole activating complex (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on structural data.

claim: Near-cognate tRNAs do not trigger (p)ppGpp synthesis.
source: Near-cognate tRNAs do not trigger (p)ppGpp synthesis (Haseltine and Block, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The tRNA accommodation model predicts that near-cognate tRNAs would sample conformations similar to those in Structures II or III, but do not proceed to the domain-closed 'acceptance' state (Structure IV).
source: Our tRNA accommodation model predicts that near-cognate tRNAs would sample conformations similar to those in Structures II or III, but do not proceed to the domain-closed 'acceptance' state (Structure IV).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural data and prior biochemical studies.

claim: Structure IV, with an accommodated cognate tRNA anticodon stem loop and closed decoding center, is necessary to activate RelA.
source: Thus, we propose that Structure IV, with an accommodated cognate tRNA anticodon stem loop and closed decoding center, is necessary to activate RelA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: The space in which the N-terminal domains are located between the sarcin-ricin loop and the spur is more constricted in the domain-closed state.
source: Notably, the space in which the N-terminal domains are located between the sarcin-ricin loop and the spur is more constricted in the domain-closed state, highlighting the possible role of interactions between these domains and ribosomal RNA in (p)ppGpp-synthetase activation.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: Two studies reported RelA-bound structures of the 70S ribosome in the presence of a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog and GTP after submission of this manuscript.
source: After submission of this manuscript, two studies reported RelA-bound structures of the 70S ribosome in the presence of a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog and GTP (Arenz et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about subsequent publications.

claim: The published complexes describe substrate-bound states of RelA, whereas the complex in this work lacks ATP and GTP and describes RelA states prior to substrate binding.
source: As such, the published complexes describe substrate-bound states of RelA, whereas our complex lacks ATP and GTP and, therefore, describes RelA states prior to substrate binding.
evidence: This is a comparison with subsequent publications.

claim: In both published studies, a single predominant global structure is reported, however the conformational variability in the 30S domains and N-terminal domains of RelA is noted.
source: In both published studies, a single predominant global structure is reported, however the conformational variability in the 30S domains (Brown et al., 2016) and N-terminal domains of RelA (Arenz et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2016) is noted, consistent with our observations.
evidence: This is a comparison with subsequent publications.

claim: The predominance of the single ribosome conformation in the published studies is likely due to the use of the antibiotic paromomycin, which stabilizes a domain-closed 30S conformation, or to the use of RelA substrate analogs, or to differences in cryo-EM dataset sizes or in classification procedures.
source: The predominance of the single ribosome conformation is likely due to the use of the antibiotic paromomycin in one study (Brown et al., 2016), which stabilizes a domain-closed 30S conformation (Ogle et al., 2001) similar to our Structure IV, or to the use of RelA substrate analogs, or to differences in cryo-EM dataset sizes or in classification procedures.
evidence: This is speculation about differences with subsequent publications.
